title: Community model adoption: scope boundaries, compatibility manifest spec, and acceptance checklist
creator: Sofia Alvarez
description:
Problem: We routinely receive community open-model submissions that vary widely in packaging, tokenizer mappings, checkpoint semantics, and supported deployment profiles. This creates friction for product teams who expect predictable pinning semantics, consistent fallback behavior, and reliable compatibility notes in the catalog.

Goal: Define a minimally sufficient "compatibility manifest" and onboarding scope so new open models can be onboarded with clear pin semantics, automated QA gates, and concise compatibility notes in the model catalog entry. The manifest should support automated validation in our intake pipeline and set expectations for runtime teams about kernel/quantization compatibility.

Scope (in-scope):
- A manifest schema (JSON/YAML) capturing required fields: model_id, canonical_version, tokenizer_family, max_sequence_length, supported_precision (fp32,int8,q4), recommended_quantization_profile, kv-cache-behavior, known-incompatible-ops, license, upstream-source, provenance-hash, test-checksum, and rollback_fallback_policy.
- Pinning semantics: define canonical_version vs. build-specific checksums; catalog shows pinned_version + acceptable_patch_range. Pins must be reversible and have a fallback variant in the catalog.
- Automated intake checks: license scanning, tokenizer mapping validation, end-to-end inference smoke tests (latency and correctness on a small reference prompt set), and security artifact checks.
- Compatibility notes template for UI: a short summary, highlighted incompatibilities (kernel/sequence limit/quantization), suggested runtime config, and recommended fallback model variants.
- Acceptance criteria for product and runtime teams, and a sample Confluence onboarding checklist.

Out of scope: auto-conversion of community weights into our canonical format, heavy performance benchmarking, and upstream model reward/quality evaluations beyond the smoke test set. Those will be follow-up projects owned by Research/Serving teams.

Trade-offs and decisions so far: we will require a minimal manifest (not a full spec) to reduce onboarding friction while still providing machine-readable hints for automation. We prioritize safety and license compliance over automatic ingestion of models missing provenance.

Next steps: finalize manifest schema with ENG and Design, implement intake validator, and wire catalog UI to surface the compatibility notes and pinned-version metadata.
acceptance_criteria: Manifest spec published in Confluence: includes required fields and example manifests for a small Llama-family and an MPT-style family.
Intake validator implemented in the intake pipeline: rejects submissions missing required manifest fields with a clear error payload.
License scanner integrated: community model submissions must pass allowed-license checks or be flagged for manual review.
Smoke test harness runs end-to-end inference on the submitted weights and reports pass/fail with latency and correctness checks recorded in the intake report.
Catalog UI displays 'pinned_version', 'acceptable_patch_range', and a one-line compatibility summary for each newly onboarded community model.

Rollback policy enforced: for each pinned version, catalog entry includes at least one fallback variant (e.g., quantized/earlier release) and runtime routing rules can use it automatically on mismatch or performance regression.
Documentation: a one-page onboarding checklist plus example PR template for community model intake is available and linked from the catalog entry flow.
Security review tickbox: intake marks models that require an HSM/KMS or additional security review; flagged models cannot be published to catalog without approval.
